title: Fusion quantization stability field notes
body:
Purpose:
Quick field notes from a week of tests investigating tail-latency instability observed when serving quantized models on fused-op execution paths (FlashAttention + paged attention mix). Goal is to capture experiments, reproducible commands, raw observations and concrete next steps for mitigation experiments.

Summary of the problem (high level):
- In mixed workloads (short chat messages ~ 8-32 tokens interleaved with longer completions 128-512), we saw a non-deterministic tail-latency spike (95th–99.9th) when the runtime switched between fused-op FlashAttention kernels and paged attention kernels under quantized execution (INT8/INT4 profiles).
- Float16 fused-op path is stable; quantized fused-op path increases jitter and occasional +20–60ms latency spikes per-request on A100-like hardware at 2048 max_batch tokens.
- Spike frequency correlates with sequence-length variance and kernel-switching events (handshake points).

Quick win hypothesis (what we think is happening):
1) Kernel handshake overhead + small CUDA stream stalls when switching from paged->flash fused kernels combined with quantization prep (repacking/scale tables) creates transient stalls that blow up tail latency for a small % of requests.
2) Quantized fused kernels expose data alignment sensitivity; misaligned tensor strides in paged-backed KV cache force additional copy/permute before kernel entry. That copy sometimes runs on a default stream and blocks the compute stream.
3) Heisenbug amplification: small noise in scheduler -> different kernel selection -> different prefetch patterns -> occasional bank conflicts -> longer kernel priming time.

What we ran (environment):
- Service binary: serving-runtime@main (commit 3f2a8b1)
- Model: openlm/llama-13b (converted), quantization profiles: int8_dynamic_v1, int4_apex_like
- Hardware: G5/ A100 40GB cluster (internal perf lab), CUDA 12.1, cuBLASLt + custom fused kernels
- Tracing: tracebench v0.9 with token-level annotations, nvtx markers around kernel selection, perf counters via nsys snapshots for sampled cases

Repro commands (short):
- run tracebench workload: ./bench/tracebench --profile=seqmix-8-32-128-512.json --runtime=serving-runtime:local --quant=int8_dynamic_v1 --kernel-policy=auto --samples=10000 --output=trace-seqmix-int8.json
- microbench single-request: ./scripts/bench/single_request_latency.sh --seq 128 --quant int8 --kernel flash --repeat 5000
- kernel level: python tools/kernel_probe.py --op attn --kernel-candidates flash,paged --quant int8 --dump-telemetry /tmp/kprobe.json

Experiment matrix (short):
- Sequence mix: {uniform-8, seqmix-8-32-128-512, long-only-512}
- Quant modes: {fp16, int8_dynamic_v1, int4_apex_like}
- Kernel policy: {force-flash, force-paged, auto-with-hysteresis}
- Batching: {small-batch (N<8), large-batch (N>64), dynamic}
- KV cache reuse: {cold-start, warm-cache}

Notable results (numbers are median across 3 runs unless otherwise noted):
- Baseline: fp16 + force-flash on seqmix => p50=12ms, p95=18ms, p99=26ms, p99.9=39ms (stable)
- int8 + force-flash on seqmix => p50=11ms, p95=25ms, p99=48ms, p99.9=95ms (spikes observed)
- int8 + force-paged on seqmix => p50=13ms, p95=22ms, p99=32ms, p99.9=45ms (better tail than force-flash-int8)
- int8 + auto-policy-without-hysteresis => intermittent 40–120ms outliers aligned with kernel switch timestamps in trace logs
- int8 + auto-policy + 200ms hysteresis on kernel choice => p99.9 reduces by ~60% vs auto-without-hysteresis
- long-only 512, int8 force-flash => stable and similar to fp16, indicates problem arises with mixed sequence-length traffic

Observations from traces and nsys snapshots:
- When kernel-switch occurs, nvtx shows: a small memcpy (device->device or host staging) occurs on default stream prior to fused kernel launch. In several samples memcpy duration ~ 12–30ms depending on layer size and alignment.
- The memcpy is often triggered by quantized kernel path that requires repacking scale tensors or applying per-channel scales into a contiguous scratch buffer. That repack currently uses a generic fallback that is not pinned to the same compute stream as the kernel.
- CUDA stream synchronization points are implicit in our dispatcher: kernel selector issues an event then submits kernel to compute stream; the fallback repack uses a different stream and calls cudaEventSynchronize in the selector. This synchrony pattern can serialize work unexpectedly.
- Small examples show bank-conflict-like increases in L2 miss rate when stride%64 != 0 for KV tensors; that correlates with slower kernel priming times for the first token after switch.

Immediate mitigations we tested and results:
- Move repack work to same compute stream as kernel (in-process experiment): reduced p99.9 from 95ms to ~55ms for int8 force-flash (good but not perfect).
- Increase hysteresis threshold for kernel switching (200ms window): reduced number of switches by ~60% and p99.9 reduced accordingly.
- Alignment enforcement: ensure KV allocations are 256B aligned and pad tensors to 64-stride multiples: reduced occurrence of large-copy events; some perf gain but introduces ~3% memory overhead.

Trade-offs noted:
- Forcing paged kernels removes the spike but increases median latency by ~10–15% for workloads that benefit from flash fused ops (long sequences).
- Alignment padding buys stability but slightly increases memory pressure; not ideal for memory-constrained Dedicated nodes.

Open hypotheses to validate:
- The repack copy could be optimized away by using lazy views + kernel-level scale application; confirm feasibility with fused op authors.
- There might be a rare path where quantization extractions rely on host->device staging buffers that are allocated in a non-pinned manner causing page fault overhead. Need to inspect allocator traces (heaptrack/pmem).
- Possible CUDA driver interactions: stream priority inversion when default stream memcpy interleaves with high-priority compute stream on certain driver versions. Need to rerun on CUDA 12.4 lab nodes.

Next experiments (actionable):
1) Implement and benchmark a prototype that applies scale adjustments inside the fused kernel (no separate repack kernel). Coordinate with fused-ops owners (PR referenced in linked_artifacts). Target: microbench p99.9 < 50ms for seqmix int8.
2) Add an allocator tracepoints experiment: enable pinned allocator for repack scratch buffers and re-run failing tracecases.
3) Long soak: deploy auto-policy + 200ms hysteresis in a canary pool for 24h with seqmix traffic generator to measure real-flavor regression rate.
4) Add finer-grained telemetry hooks: record kernel candidate list, selected kernel id, alignment flags, and stream id on events so we can correlate spikes to specific layers/keys.
5) Consider a fallback policy: for quantized fused kernels, require warm-cache threshold (e.g., after K warm calls) before allowing fuse path in mixed traffic.

Notes to implementers / TODOs:
- Diego: prototype in kernel dispatcher to move repack to compute stream (in progress branch: feat/repack-on-compute)
- Priya: add telemetry fields to token trace schema to include "kernel_candidate_set" and "alignment_flag" (Linear ticket RW-2109)
- Samira: schedule 12.4 driver nodes in perf lab and re-run the top 10 failing tracecases, capture nsys + nvprof snapshots

Misc fragile details observed (handy troubleshooting tips):
- When reproducing locally, use small jitter in client arrival times; perfectly synthetic uniform spacing hides the problem.
- Use --samples >= 5k to surface 99.9th spikes; smaller samples can miss them entirely.
- Dump per-layer first-invocation times; the spike often appears on the first large-attn layer after a kernel switch.

Concluding thought:
This appears to be an interaction between (1) quantization repack patterns, (2) kernel selection/handshake streams and (3) alignment/stride sensitivity of fused kernels. We have several promising mitigations (repack-on-compute, hysteresis, alignment padding) with immediate gains. Next priority is to implement in a branch a kernel-level scale apply (the lowest-overhead fix) and to add richer telemetry so we can be confident in production rollouts.

Attachments/logs (local): /perf/artifacts/fusion-quant-2025-02-10/* (trace jsons, nsys captures, kprobe dumps)

If you pick this up: start with the repack-on-compute prototype and the telemetry work; both are high ROI and small risk.
